svg.aria-label: The two meters behind the Redshift or Athena decision: Athena bills bytes scanned with a ten megabyte floor per query and nothing when idle, Redshift Serverless bills RPU-seconds with a sixty second floor per usage and bills any query that reaches the endpoint, the exchange rate between the two at seventy five gigabytes of scanning per RPU-hour, the fact that both engines now sell both meters, and the three ways each meter runs away from you
svg.title: Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift are usually compared on price per query, which hides the fact that they meter different things. Athena bills the bytes a query reads, at five dollars per terabyte scanned, rounded up to the nearest megabyte with a ten megabyte minimum per query, and bills nothing at all between queries. Redshift Serverless bills the time a warehouse is awake, at zero point three seven five dollars per RPU-hour metered per second with a sixty second minimum charge, and treats every query that reaches the endpoint as billable, including the lightweight health checks a connection pool sends. The two meters convert at one exchange rate: zero point three seven five divided by five is zero point zero seven five terabytes, so one RPU-hour costs the same money as scanning seventy five gigabytes. An hour of the smallest serverless warehouse, four RPUs, costs one dollar fifty, or three hundred gigabytes of scanning. Eight RPUs for an hour costs three dollars, or six hundred gigabytes. The console default of one hundred and twenty eight RPUs costs forty eight dollars an hour, or nine point six terabytes of scanning every hour it stays awake. Four ra3.4xlarge nodes at three dollars twenty six an hour each cost thirteen dollars and four cents an hour, or two point six terabytes. Neither engine is purely one meter any more: Athena sells capacity reservations from a minimum of four data processing units at thirty cents per DPU-hour, which is one dollar twenty an hour, or zero point two four terabytes of scanning, and Redshift Serverless sells per-second usage. So the decision is not which meter is cheaper but what the engine gives you besides running the SQL: managed storage with sort and distribution keys, materialized views, real transactions, concurrency scaling and a stable endpoint on the warehouse side, against no idle cost, no endpoint to keep warm, partition projection and query result reuse on the lake side. Each meter has three ways of running away from you. Athena bills a ten megabyte minimum on every query however small, so a dashboard firing thousands of tiny queries pays the floor thousands of times, and a cancelled query is still charged. Redshift Serverless bills the sixty second minimum on a warehouse woken by a health check, keeps scaled capacity for a period after load falls, and bills an open transaction until the session times out after six hours.

g.text: Two meters, one exchange rate
The question is not which engine is cheaper. It is which meter your demand shape happens to run.
1. What each service actually meters
Athena — bytes a query reads
$5/TB scanned, rounded up to the nearest megabyte
Floor: 10 MB minimum per query — about $0.00005
Between queries the meter is off. There is no endpoint,
nothing to pause, and nothing to forget to pause.
A cancelled query is still charged for what it read.
Redshift Serverless — time a warehouse is awake
$0.375 per RPU-hour, metered on a per-second basis
Floor: 60-second minimum charge — $0.05 at 8 RPUs
Every query that reaches the endpoint is billable, including
a connection pool’s SELECT 1 health check.
Storage is billed separately at $0.024/GB-Month.
2. The exchange rate: $0.375 per RPU-hour divided by $5 per TB is 0.075 TB
One RPU-hour costs the same money as scanning 75 GB. So an hour of warehouse, priced in Athena:
4 RPUs (the smallest base capacity)
$1.50 / hour
= 0.3 TB scanned
8 RPUs
$3.00 / hour
= 0.6 TB scanned
128 RPUs — the console default, if nobody changes it
= 9.6 TB scanned, every hour
4 x ra3.4xlarge provisioned, at $3.26 per node-hour
= 2.6 TB scanned
Read the right-hand column as a budget, not a benchmark: it is what the same money buys on the other meter.
3. Neither engine is one meter any more — so the meter is not the decision
Athena also sells time
Capacity reservations: minimum 4 DPUs at $0.30 per DPU hour
$1.20 / hour = 0.24 TB scanned, whether queried or not
Buys concurrency control, not a different query engine.
What the warehouse sells that the lake does not
Sort and distribution keys, materialized views, transactions,
concurrency scaling, WLM queues, a stable JDBC endpoint
That list, not the price per query, is the actual decision.
4. How each meter runs away from you
Thousands of small queries each pay the 10 MB floor
An unpartitioned table turns every filter into a full read
The workgroup alert notifies; only the per-query limit cancels
A health check wakes the warehouse and pays 60 seconds
Scaled capacity can stay high for a period after load falls
An open transaction bills until the session times out at 6 hours
